findings.title: Async legacy writes inherit the request context and are canceled after the handler returns
findings.body: `Create` starts a goroutine that derives from the caller's `ctx` (`context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)`). The same pattern is used in `Delete` (line 110), `Update` (line 135), and `DeleteCollection` (line 163). In the apiserver this `ctx` is the HTTP request context, which is canceled when `ServeHTTP` returns; the dual writer returns immediately after starting the goroutine, so the legacy write races with cancellation and can be canceled before it has completed. Since the legacy write is the safety mechanism for Mode 3, this can silently lose the backup write. Use a request-detached context such as `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)` plus an explicit timeout, or a server-owned background context.

findings.title: Unordered goroutines can leave stale data in legacy storage
findings.body: Each successful storage write launches an independent goroutine for the legacy write, with no per-object queue, mutex, version check, or ordering guarantee. Two concurrent updates or deletes for the same object can complete in unified storage in one order but be applied to legacy in the opposite order due to goroutine scheduling. For example, an older `Update` goroutine can run after a newer one, leaving legacy with the older object even though unified storage has the newer one. A per-key worker, resourceVersion precondition, or other ordered writeback mechanism is needed to ensure the legacy backup does not regress.

findings.title: Legacy Update recomputes the update instead of writing the object returned by unified storage
findings.body: `d.Legacy.Update(ctx, name, objInfo, ...)` passes the original `rest.UpdatedObjectInfo` to legacy storage. `UpdatedObjectInfo` is called again by legacy storage against the legacy old object, so it can produce a different object than `res` returned by `d.Storage.Update`, especially when legacy and unified storage are at different versions. The previous implementation wrapped the already-returned unified object (`updateWrapper{updated: obj}`), ensuring legacy wrote the same object. Reinstate that behavior by passing a wrapper that returns `res`; otherwise the legacy backup may be inconsistent with unified storage or fail update validation.

findings.title: Storage Create failure is recorded as a legacy duration
findings.body: On `d.Storage.Create` error, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...)` using `startStorage`. This increments the legacy error/duration metric for an operation in which legacy was never called, while the unified-storage error is not recorded as a storage duration. It should call `d.recordStorageDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage)`. The same mistake exists in `Update` at line 129.

findings.title: Delete success records the object name in the `kind` metric label
findings.body: After a successful `Storage.Delete`, the code calls `d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage)`, passing `name` where every other call passes `options.Kind`. The `kind` label will contain per-object names instead of the resource kind, producing unbounded metric cardinality and destroying aggregation by kind. It should pass `options.Kind`.

findings.title: Legacy DeleteCollection result is recorded as a storage duration
findings.body: In `DeleteCollection`'s legacy goroutine, `d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, ..., startLegacy)` uses the storage metric for the legacy call and starts from `startLegacy`. This mislabels legacy duration/errors as unified-storage operations and leaves the legacy metric unpopulated. It should call `d.recordLegacyDuration(err != nil, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startLegacy)`.

findings.title: Mode3 unit tests never wait for or assert the asynchronous legacy write
findings.body: The success tests configure legacy mock expectations (for example, `setupLegacyFn` in `TestMode3_Create`) but return immediately after the synchronous unified-storage call. Because the actual legacy write happens in a goroutine, the test passes even if the legacy mock is never called, and no `m.AssertExpectations` or synchronization verifies it. This makes the core Mode3 behavior (legacy backup write) untested and can also leave background goroutines running after the subtest exits. Add a wait group or injectable async executor and assert the legacy calls.

findings.title: Mode3 integration tests reuse synchronous CRUD assertions and race with legacy writeback
findings.body: The new Mode3 cases call `doPlaylistTests`, which checks the legacy API immediately after k8s create/update/delete (for example `client.Resource.Create` followed by a legacy `/api/playlists` GET, and `client.Resource.Delete` followed by a legacy GET). With Mode3 those legacy writes are asynchronous, so the test assertions are timing-dependent and can fail intermittently if the goroutine has not completed. Mode3 needs a poll/wait mechanism for the legacy side or a separate test suite that accounts for asynchronous propagation.
